plan.topic: Can pneumonic plague spread person to person? Close-contact respiratory droplets vs long-range airborne spread (measles, COVID)
plan.angle: Answer within 10s: 'Yes, but mainly through close, face-to-face contact with someone already sick with pneumonic plague and coughing (CDC, WHO). It doesn't hang in the air of a room the way measles can (CDC: up to 2 hours).' COVID gets one line, comparing its easier indoor shared-air spread, without claiming parity with measles. Bubonic plague from flea bites rarely spreads between people. That's why tracing a defined group of contacts works, plus preventive antibiotics when clinicians and health authorities advise them. Status line: 'As of Oct 7, 2026: Russian officials told WHO no plague case has been recorded. Tests on contacts found no dangerous pathogens, and WHO says testing on the cause of death continues and rates the risk low for Russia.' Close with 'If you're worried, talk to a health professional.' Point to L1. 35–50s.
plan.working_title: Can Pneumonic Plague Spread Person to Person? #shorts
plan.why: Spin-off of L1. Contagion is the most-asked question in every explainer, and this uses our proven search-question formula with named comparators. | fact-check: The core science is sound. CDC and WHO both say pneumonic plague spreads mainly through respiratory droplets during close contact with an ill, coughing person, and that bubonic plague rarely passes between people. Two fixes are needed. (1) The status line 'Russian authorities say no plague found' overstates what's known. Russia says no plague case was recorded and testing of contacts found no dangerous pathogens. WHO says lab testing to confirm the cause of death is still under way and rates the risk low for Russia overall. (2) The comparator framing must be accurate. Measles is the clear long-range airborne example: CDC says it can linger in the air for up to 2 hours. COVID-19 spreads by both respiratory droplets and aerosols, and mostly at close range. So don't say COVID spreads 'long-range like measles'. Present measles as the airborne contrast, and COVID as 'spreads more easily through shared indoor air'. Say 'usually' or 'mainly', not absolutes.

Can pneumonic plague spread person to person? Here's what CDC and WHO say.

• Pneumonic plague spreads mainly through close contact with respiratory droplets from a coughing patient (CDC).
• That's not the same as measles, which can linger in the air up to 2 hours after an infected person leaves (CDC), or COVID, which spreads more easily through shared indoor air (WHO).
• Bubonic plague (from flea bites) rarely spreads between people.
• Because pneumonic plague needs close contact, health teams can trace contacts and offer preventive antibiotics when authorities advise it.

Status as of Oct 6, 2026: the Irkutsk lab worker's death was reported as suspected pneumonic plague. Russia told WHO no plague case has been recorded, and contacts tested so far show no dangerous pathogens. WHO says the cause of death isn't officially confirmed yet; testing continues. WHO-stated risk: moderate-to-low for Irkutsk, low for Russia, very low for the WHO European Region.

script.hook_pattern: The opening line asks the search question and answers it ("Yes, mainly up close"). Next comes CDC's point that close contact is required. Measles is the named airborne contrast, with CDC's "up to 2 hours". COVID gets one line on shared indoor air. Then the payoff: why close-range spread can be traced. The dated status is split into two attributed scenes: the suspected case and Russia's report, then WHO's pending confirmation and its risk ratings by area. The ending gives the worried/urgent-care line and loops back to the opening question. The fact-checker's fixes push the narration to 170 words, about 80–85 seconds.

factcheck.summary:
I checked all 7 sources and each one exists and supports the line it's cited for. Every claim in the Short is accurate, and the framing and safety are good.

- **Plague spread (CDC, 15 May 2024):** droplets from someone with plague pneumonia need direct, close contact, and droplets are the only way plague spreads between people. The WHO fact sheet (updated 29 Sep 2026) says spread between people of bubonic plague is rare and that pneumonic plague spreads through respiratory particles.
- **Measles (CDC, 29 Apr 2026):** the virus can live up to 2 hours in an airspace.
- **COVID (WHO, 2021):** aerosols can stay in the air in poorly ventilated indoor spaces.
- **Preventive antibiotics (CDC):** recommended for close (under 6 ft), sustained contact. The script correctly says to take them only when health authorities advise, with no drugs or doses named.
- **Status line (UN News/WHO and NBC, Oct 6):** Russian authorities reported no plague case, no dangerous pathogens were found in contacts, and the cause of death isn't confirmed yet. WHO rates the risk moderate to low for Irkutsk, low for the Russian Federation and very low for the WHO European Region. NBC says about 60% of contacts had been tested, so "tested so far" is the right hedge.

Three small wording fixes:
1. The status scene never says what the case was suspected to be.
2. The closing line could carry the urgency the guardrail requires.
3. "Europe" should read "WHO European Region". Nothing here would mislead a viewer.

issues.claim: As of Oct 6, 2026, Russian officials told WHO no plague case was recorded... WHO says testing on the cause of death continues.
issues.problem: Viewers coming from the feed get no context: the scene never says the death was reported as suspected pneumonic plague, or that the cause of death hasn't been officially confirmed (WHO's wording). Without that, 'no plague case recorded' could be heard as plague having been ruled out.
issues.fix: Narration: "As of Oct 6, 2026, a lab worker's death in Irkutsk was reported as suspected pneumonic plague. Russian officials told WHO no plague case was recorded, and contacts tested so far showed no dangerous pathogens. WHO says the cause of death isn't officially confirmed and testing continues. It rates the risk moderate to low for Irkutsk, low for Russia overall, and very low for the WHO European Region." List item 3: "WHO: cause of death not yet confirmed, testing continues".

issues.problem: WHO's assessment covers the WHO European Region, which is wider than 'Europe'. That's a small scope difference.
issues.fix: Narration: replace "very low for Europe" with "very low for the WHO European Region". On-screen list item: "WHO risk: moderate to low (Irkutsk), low (Russia), very low (WHO Europe region)".

audio.soundNotes: Music sits at -13.5 dB under voice (in range) and only -18.2 dB in pauses (a bit low against the -14 target), so I nudged the overall music gain up slightly (x1.1) rather than further — ducking plus ambient voice already protect intelligibility, and pushing harder would risk breaching the under-voice ceiling. Cues are mostly well-placed; I muted a dozen redundant simultaneous layers (duplicate tick/whip/whoosh fired alongside a swell/pop/swoosh at the same timestamp) to respect the 3-4-sounds-per-second rule, especially in the dense "chips" cluster near 36s. Trimmed two cues that spiked over dialogue (swoosh at 39.4s and 54.3s, which measured -9/-6 dB against voice) down to a felt level, nudged two mildly hot cues (2.5s intro swoosh, 54s blip) down a touch, and restored the near-silent closing swell at 87s so the outro doesn't vanish. Added 5 bespoke, sparing cues (opening tension drone, night-air texture for the airborne-survival stat, a capsule click for preventive antibiotics, a document-stamp for the WHO report line, and a slow reassuring heartbeat under the "call a doctor" line) to add felt texture at key story beats without ever competing with the narration, consistent with keeping SFX thin on the serious, doctor-advice moment.
